title: “DO NOT DEPRIVE ONE ANOTHER”: The Marriage-Bed Verse That Can Be Dangerously Misused
paragraphs: “DO NOT DEPRIVE ONE ANOTHER”: The Marriage-Bed Verse That Can Be Dangerously Misused

What if one of the Bible’s most intimate instructions was never meant to give a spouse permission to demand—but to teach husband and wife how radically mutual, tender, and Christ-shaped marriage is supposed to become?
There are Bible verses that comfort us.
There are Bible verses that confront us.

And then there are Bible verses that become dangerous when someone tears a few words out of their context, puts God’s name behind a selfish desire, and uses Scripture to silence the person they promised to love.
“Do not deprive one another.”
Five words.
They can sound simple.
Until they are spoken in a bedroom where someone is exhausted.
Until they are quoted to a wife who is frightened.
Until they are thrown at a husband who is grieving.
Until Scripture becomes leverage.
Until “God says you owe me” replaces tenderness, patience, conversation, prayer, and love.
And suddenly a passage intended to protect marital faithfulness can be twisted into something Paul never wrote.
So before another wounded husband or wife hears 1 Corinthians 7:5 used like a divine demand for sexual access, we need to open the Bible carefully.
Not to weaken Scripture.
To let Scripture speak more completely.
Paul writes in Greek:
Μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλους.
“Do not deprive one another.”
But keep reading.
εἰ μήτι ἂν ἐκ συμφώνου πρὸς καιρόν…
“…except perhaps by mutual agreement for a time…”
That expression matters enormously.
ἐκ συμφώνου — ek symphōnou.
By agreement.
Together.
The word is related to the idea of being in accord—of voices sounding together rather than one voice overpowering another.
And notice something else Paul refuses to let us miss:
ἀλλήλους — allēlous.
“One another.”
Paul does not write, “Wives, do not deprive your husbands.”
He says to one another.
Then look at the astonishing symmetry surrounding the verse.
“The husband should fulfill his marital duty to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband.”
The Greek contains that crucial word:
ὁμοίως — homoiōs.
Likewise.
In the same manner.

And Paul continues with language that would have been striking in his ancient context: the wife does not exercise authority over her body alone, but her husband does—and then Paul immediately reverses the statement.
The husband does not exercise authority over his body alone either.
His wife does.
Paul refuses to create a one-way sexual entitlement.
He places husband and wife under reciprocal obligation.
That changes the atmosphere of the passage.
This is not:
“You belong to me, therefore I can take.”
It is closer to:
“I belong to you too, therefore I cannot live as though my desires are the only desires that matter.”
Marriage does not transform selfishness into holiness merely because selfishness now wears a wedding ring.
Christian marriage is supposed to crucify selfishness.
That is why this passage becomes dangerous when someone reads “do not deprive” while ignoring “one another,” “likewise,” and “by mutual agreement.”
Imagine a husband saying, “Your body belongs to me.”
Paul would force him to finish the sentence.
Your body also belongs in covenantal responsibility to her.
That means the verse cannot honestly be used as a blank check for coercion.
It cannot faithfully mean, “My desire automatically overrules your fear.”
It cannot faithfully mean, “Your exhaustion is irrelevant.”
It cannot faithfully mean, “Because we are married, you are forbidden from saying that something hurts.”
It cannot mean that sickness, trauma, postpartum recovery, disability, emotional distress, medication effects, relational wounds, or genuine physical pain suddenly become spiritually meaningless.
And it certainly cannot mean that force becomes righteous because the people involved exchanged vows.
There is a difference between Paul teaching married Christians not to weaponize prolonged sexual withdrawal against each other and someone weaponizing Paul to obtain sex.
Those are not the same thing.
In fact, the second can become the very opposite of the love Scripture commands.
Biblical intimacy is not merely about obtaining access to another person’s body.
It is about covenant.
Trust.
Giving.
Knowing.
Tenderness.
Faithfulness.
Safety.
Self-control.
Sacrifice.
And love.
That last word changes everything.
Because Christian marriage cannot be interpreted apart from Christ.
The New Testament does not tell husbands to imitate domination.
It points them toward Jesus.
“Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
Christlike love asks a terrifying question of our selfishness:
What am I willing to give up for the good of the person I love?
Jesus did not reveal love by exploiting vulnerability.
He revealed love by giving Himself.
That is the shape Christian marriage is supposed to take.

So if your interpretation of a marriage-bed passage produces entitlement without sacrifice, authority without tenderness, demands without listening, and gratification without concern for the other person’s wellbeing, something has gone terribly wrong in the interpretation.
Because Jesus does not teach us to ask only:
“What am I entitled to receive?”
Jesus teaches us to ask:
“How can I love?”
And maybe that is where this becomes uncomfortable for everyone.
Because misuse of this passage can happen in more than one direction.
One spouse can weaponize the verse to demand intimacy.
Another can weaponize withdrawal to punish, manipulate, humiliate, or control.
Neither reflects the heart of covenant love.
Paul’s words confront both.
Do not use sex as a weapon.
Do not use Scripture as a weapon.
Do not use rejection as a weapon.
Do not use desire as a weapon.
Do not turn the marriage bed into a courtroom where one spouse is permanently prosecuting the other.
Talk.
Listen.
Pray.
Repent.
Seek help when necessary.
Ask what is happening beneath the surface.
Because sometimes “not tonight” is not rejection.
Sometimes it means:
“I am hurting.”
Sometimes:
“I am afraid.”
Sometimes:
“My body has changed and I don’t know how to tell you.”
Sometimes:
“I still love you, but something between us is broken.”
Sometimes:
“I need tenderness before I can feel close again.”
Sometimes:
“What happened to me years ago is still living inside my nervous system.”
And sometimes the spouse hearing those words has wounds too.
“I miss you.”
“I feel unwanted.”
“I don’t know how to tell you how lonely I have become.”
“I’m afraid you don't desire me anymore.”
“I feel ashamed for even wanting you.”
These are not problems healed by throwing verses across the bed like grenades.
They need truth spoken in love.
They need patience.
They need repentance where sin exists.
They may need pastoral care, medical care, or qualified professional counseling.
Sometimes they need tears.
Sometimes forgiveness.
Sometimes difficult boundaries.
Sometimes protection.
Sometimes a long rebuilding of trust.
But they need Christ in the room.
Because marriage is not healed merely when two bodies occupy the same bed.
Marriage begins healing when two hearts stop hiding.
And for the person reading this who has been spiritually manipulated with this passage, hear the distinction clearly:
The Bible is not the abuser.
The misuse of the Bible is.
Jesus is not honored when Scripture is twisted to excuse cruelty.
Christ does not need distortion to defend holiness.
Truth can withstand context.
And perhaps someone reading this has carried secret shame for years because you were told that being a “godly spouse” meant never expressing pain, fear, exhaustion, or boundaries.
Maybe you thought God was angry every time your body froze.
Maybe someone quoted Paul while refusing to imitate Jesus.
Please read Paul again.
Read all the words.
ἀλλήλους.
One another.
ὁμοίως.
Likewise.
ἐκ συμφώνου.
By mutual agreement.
There is reciprocity running through this passage.
There is responsibility running both directions.
And there is something else we desperately need to recover.
Sexual intimacy in Christian marriage is not supposed to resemble a commercial transaction.
It is not “I performed my duty, now you owe me.”
It is covenantal self-giving.
That is precisely why selfishness can corrupt it from either side.
Marriage says:
I will not casually neglect you.
I will not manipulate you.
I will not punish you with my body.
I will not demand your body while ignoring your soul.
I will not reduce you to what you can give me.
I will learn you.
I will hear you.
I will bring my desires honestly before you.
I will care about your desires too.
I will seek your good.
And when sin enters this marriage—and it will, because two sinners live here—we will keep bringing our brokenness to Jesus.
That is the part pornography never teaches.
That is the part entitlement cannot understand.
That is the part selfishness hates.
Real intimacy requires vulnerability.
And vulnerability cannot flourish where fear rules the room.
Perhaps this article is exposing something uncomfortable in you.
Maybe you have quoted this passage selfishly.
Maybe you have pressured your spouse.
Maybe you have dismissed their pain.
Maybe you have used withdrawal deliberately to punish them.
Maybe resentment has been sleeping between you for years.
Maybe you have been pretending everything is fine because admitting the truth feels terrifying.
Then this is not an invitation to condemnation.
It is an invitation to repentance.
Jesus Christ did not go to the cross merely to make guilty people feel worse.
He went to save sinners.
People like us.
Controlling sinners.
Selfish sinners.
Wounded sinners.
Sexually broken sinners.
Ashamed sinners.
Religious sinners.
Secretly bitter sinners.
People who have hurt others.
People who have been hurt by others.
At Calvary, Jesus did not excuse sin.
He bore sin.
And because He rose again, your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Repentance can begin tonight.
An apology can begin tonight.
Truth can begin tonight.
“I was wrong.”
“I pressured you.”
“I stopped listening.”
“I used rejection to hurt you.”
“I have been hiding.”
“I need help.”
“Will you forgive me?”
“Can we pray?”
Those may not sound dramatic.
But sometimes resurrection begins with a sentence whispered through tears.
You do not have to tell strangers private details. Simply comment, “Jesus, teach me to love like You,” or “Christ is still healing me.”
Let believers pray instead of pretending believers never struggle.
Not because every person needs to know the private details of your marriage.
Someone may be living under religious guilt God never commanded.
Someone else may be neglecting their spouse and calling it spirituality.
Someone may desperately need to discover that biblical marriage is neither coercion nor manipulation but covenantal, mutual, Christ-shaped love.
Marriage has seasons, and you may need these words again when emotions are louder than wisdom.
It does not.
Not because money buys blessing.
It cannot.
We will not place that burden on Scripture.

The New Testament does teach that Gospel ministry may be materially supported, while also teaching that giving should come willingly rather than through compulsion. So if you have already purposed in your heart to financially support Christian teaching and discipleship, you may choose to make Gospel Warrior part of that voluntary giving.
And if financial support is not possible, please do not feel spiritually inferior.
Save these teachings.
Pray for the ministry.
There is more than one way to help truth travel.
Because ultimately this was never supposed to be about building an audience around us.
It is about pointing people toward Him.
Jesus Christ.
The Bridegroom who does not exploit His Bride but gave Himself for her.
The Savior who confronts sin without abandoning the sinner who comes to Him.
The King who enters our most embarrassing rooms and still offers redemption.

The One who can walk into a marriage scarred by selfishness, resentment, sexual brokenness, silence, manipulation, shame, or years of misunderstanding and begin writing something neither spouse believed was still possible.
Grace does not pretend the scandal never happened.
Grace meets us inside it, tells the truth about it, calls us to repent, and then places the pen into nail-scarred hands.
And maybe the most intimate question in your marriage tonight is not, “What does my spouse owe me?”
Maybe it is:
“Jesus, what would it look like for me to love this person the way You have loved me?”
Because when Christ enters the places we were most ashamed to let Him see, the bedroom does not have to remain a battlefield.
It can become another place where grace begins rewriting the story.
The verse you thought was about what you could demand may actually be calling you to remember how deeply you were called to give.
